title: Mastery Challenge: How Money Works
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of How Money Works Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree, from what money is to the big ideas economists argue about. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The How Money Works Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from Level 1's prison-camp cigarettes to the big ideas economists still argue about. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: How Money Works: mastered
learned: What money is and why people trust it
From barter and coins to gold, bank records and code
Big thinkers: Smith, Marx, Keynes, Hayek
How real people and markets behave

questions.prompt: A bakery chalks every price on its board in euros. Which job of money is that?

options.label: Store of value
options.rationale: That's keeping money to spend later.

options.label: Medium of exchange
options.rationale: That's paying with it.

options.label: Legal tender
options.rationale: That's a government declaration, not one of the three jobs.

questions.explanation: Stating prices in one common unit is money's job as a unit of account.

questions.prompt: Without money, why does a mechanic who wants lunch have a hard time?

options.label: Food is illegal to barter
options.rationale: Barter is legal; the problem is matching.

options.label: Farmers only accept gold
options.rationale: In barter there is no money at all, gold included.

options.label: He must find someone with food who also wants a repair
Mechanics are paid only in cigarettes
options.rationale: Cigarettes were money in Level 1's camp, not here.

questions.explanation: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: each side must want what the other offers.

questions.prompt: What stands behind a fiat currency like today's US dollar?

options.label: A fixed amount of gold per note
options.rationale: That link ended in 1971.

options.label: Silver coins in a government vault
options.rationale: Fiat money has no commodity backing.

options.label: The paper and ink it is printed with
options.rationale: A note costs cents to print.

options.label: A government declaring it legal tender, and people trusting it

questions.explanation: Fiat money has no value of its own; a government declares it legal tender and trust does the rest.

questions.prompt: On August 15, 1971, what did President Nixon suspend?

options.label: Foreign governments' right to swap dollars for gold
The printing of $100 bills
options.rationale: Printing continued; the gold link was the change.

options.label: All bank deposits in the US
options.rationale: Deposits were untouched.

options.label: The use of coins in shops
options.rationale: Coins stayed in use.

questions.explanation: Nixon closed the gold window, ending the dollar's last link to gold and leaving fiat money.

questions.prompt: According to Adam Smith, why does the baker have bread ready for you?

options.label: A law orders bakers to feed the town
options.rationale: Nobody orders it; self-interest does the work.

options.label: Selling to you serves the baker's own interest
The baker feels generous toward customers
options.rationale: Smith said the opposite: not benevolence.

options.label: A central planner sets the bread target
options.rationale: That's a command economy, not Smith's market.

questions.explanation: Smith: we expect our dinner from the baker's regard to his own interest, and an invisible hand turns that into shared good.

questions.prompt: What did Marx and Engels predict would happen to capitalism?

options.label: It would spread to every country and last forever
options.rationale: They predicted its end.

options.label: It would return to barter
options.rationale: They predicted revolution, not barter.

options.label: The industrial working class would overthrow it
Governments would tie it back to gold
options.rationale: Gold was not their subject.

questions.explanation: Marx and Engels predicted the industrial working class would one day overthrow capitalism.

questions.prompt: Starting in the 1970s, which school of thought eclipsed Keynesian economics?

options.label: Mercantilism
options.rationale: Smith argued against mercantilism two centuries earlier.

options.label: Behavioral economics
options.rationale: That came later and challenges rationality, not Keynes.

options.label: The gold standard
options.rationale: That's a monetary system, not a school of thought.

questions.explanation: Monetarists led by Friedman argued government should steady the economy only by growing the money supply steadily.

questions.prompt: You won't sell a sweater you never wear for what you'd pay for it. What is that called?

options.label: The invisible hand
options.rationale: That's Smith's idea about self-interest and markets.

options.label: Surplus value
options.rationale: That's Marx's term for kept profit.

options.label: An externality
options.rationale: That's a cost falling on someone outside a deal.

questions.explanation: Valuing things more because you own them is the endowment effect, which Thaler explained through loss aversion.

questions.prompt: Two rival cafés both slash prices and both earn less. Which idea explains the trap?

options.label: The double coincidence of wants
options.rationale: That's barter's matching problem.

options.label: The gold standard
options.rationale: That's about backing money with gold.

options.label: The labor theory of value
options.rationale: That's Marx's idea about where value comes from.

questions.explanation: Each café does better cutting prices whatever the other does, yet both end up worse off: the prisoner's dilemma.

questions.prompt: What did Arthur Pigou propose for activities that impose costs on others?

options.label: Banning all trade in them
options.rationale: He proposed pricing the harm, not banning trade.

options.label: Letting the invisible hand sort it out
options.rationale: Pigou wanted government to step in.

options.label: Paying them a subsidy
options.rationale: Subsidies were for activities that spread benefits.

questions.explanation: Pigou argued negative externalities should be taxed and positive ones subsidized.
